Important




Try this without AI first — struggle builds understanding.
Ask if you are stuck. Asking builds understanding too!





Download a Sentinel-2 L2A scene of your choice from the Copernicus Browser (follow the steps from the lesson slides). Extract the .zip archive and note the path to the resulting .SAFE folder.
Import the Blue (B02), Green (B03), Red (B04), and NIR (B08) bands from the IMG_DATA/R10m/ subfolder (see Spectral Bands (Wikipedia)). Convert digital numbers to surface reflectance using scale and offset manually.
After converting, plot a histogram of one band with hist() and inspect minmax(s2). What do you notice about the value range, and why does this happen? Clip all values to [0, 1] using app() and store the result back as s2.



Visualize the Sentinel-2 image as a True Color composite (Red = B04, Green = B03, Blue = B02) and a False Color composite (Red = B08/NIR, Green = B04, Blue = B03). Use plotRGB() with stretch = "histogram".
Which land cover types appear bright red in the False Color image, and why?



The SCL band is not in R10m/ — find it in the IMG_DATA/R20m/ folder of your SAFE archive using list.files() with pattern = "SCL". Import it, resample to match s2, and apply a cloud mask keeping only pixels classified as vegetation (4), bare soils (5), water (6), or snow/ice (11).
Resample the SCL to match the resolution of s2 before masking (use method = "near"). Store the result as s2_masked and report what percentage of pixels are cloud-free.



Compute NDVI from both s2 (unmasked) and s2_masked (cloud-masked):
\[\text{NDVI} = \frac{\text{B08} - \text{B04}}{\text{B08} + \text{B04}}\]
Compare the global mean NDVI of both images using global(..., mean, na.rm = TRUE). Why does the masked image have a higher mean NDVI?



Write the cloud-masked NDVI to disk in two ways:

As Float32 (full precision, no transformation)
As Byte (0–255) using scoff_params() to compute scale and offset, with DEFLATE compression

Compare the file sizes using file.size(). Then read the Byte file back and compute the maximum absolute difference from the original NDVI using global(abs(...), max, na.rm = TRUE). How large is the precision loss?

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Dataframe → Matrix
The gain from converting to a matrix:

A dataframe is a list of column vectors — each column is a separate object in memory
A matrix stores all values in one contiguous block of memory
All values have the same type (dbl) → no per-column type metadata, enables vectorized operations
Row/column names are stored once separately, not repeated

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Images are Rasters

The spatial raster data model represents the world with the continuous grid of cells (a.k.a. pixels)
This data model often refers to so-called regular grids, in which each cell has the same, constant size
Through its inherent model, this data naturally fits into the wide data structure



This connects directly to the previous lesson on wide vs long data
Emphasize that raster data is inherently a grid/matrix structure
Each pixel has a fixed location - this is why wide format makes sense
Regular grids are the foundation of most remote sensing data
We will focus on the regular grids only. However, several other types of grids exist, including rotated, sheared, rectilinear, and curvilinear grids (see Chapter 1 of Pebesma and Bivand (2023)).

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Types of raster data

Raster datasets usually represent continuous phenomena such as elevation, temperature, population density or spectral data.
Discrete features such as soil or land-cover classes can also be represented in the raster data model



Distinguish between continuous (elevation, temperature) and discrete (land cover classes) data
Both can be stored in raster format, but analysis approaches differ
Most remote sensing applications deal with continuous spectral values
Discrete classifications often result from processing continuous data

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
section: A more complex example: Spectral data
text:
A more complex example: Spectral data

Typically, RS imagery consists of more than 1 band
In this case, the data is stored in a 3 dimensional array (where band is the 3rd-dimension)
A RS image can contain any number of bands.
The most well known type of RS imagery consists of 3 Bands from the red, blue and green spectrum



Move from 2D (single band) to 3D (multi-band) concept
Each band captures different wavelengths of electromagnetic spectrum
RGB is familiar to students - good starting point
Modern satellites can have hundreds of bands (hyperspectral)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Multispectral Datasets

Multiband datasets usually capture different parts of the EM spectrum
E.g. the Landsat image from the previous example has 6 bands capturing the following wavelengths:

Band 1: Blue (0.45 - 0.52 µm)
Band 2: Green (0.52 - 0.60 µm)
Band 3: Red (0.63 - 0.69 µm)
Band 4: Near-Infrared (0.77 - 0.90 µm)
Band 5: Short-wave Infrared (1.55 - 1.75 µm)
Band 7: Mid-Infrared (2.08 - 2.35 µm)




Point out that Band 6 (thermal) is missing from this list - was not included in this dataset
Each band serves different purposes: visible for true color, NIR for vegetation health, SWIR for moisture
These wavelength ranges are carefully chosen based on atmospheric windows and target phenomena
Students will learn to use different band combinations for different applications

text:
Representations of multispectral data

A true color image is created by using the Red (3), Green (2) and Blue (1) Band and mapping these to RGB
A false color image is created by mapping other bands to RGB



True color: what our eyes would see if we were there
False color: reveals information not visible to human eye
NIR false color is very common - vegetation appears red because it reflects strongly in NIR
Different false color combinations highlight different features (water, urban areas, etc.)

Walk through each field: class, dimensions (nrow x ncol x nlyr), resolution, extent, CRS
“sources” tells us the file on disk — if in memory only, this would say “memory”
min/max are the data value range, not the spatial extent

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Querying individual components

nrow(r)   # rows (y dimension)

[1] 90

ncol(r)   # columns (x dimension)

[1] 95

nlyr(r)   # number of layers / bands

[1] 1



ext(r)    # bounding box in CRS units

SpatExtent : 5.7416666666666663, 6.5333333333333332, 49.441666666666663, 50.191666666666663 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)

res(r)    # pixel size (x, y) in CRS units

[1] 0.008333333 0.008333333




nrow × ncol = total number of pixels per band
ext() and res() together define the raster grid — if you know three, you can derive the fourth
Here, res() is in degrees because the CRS is geographic (WGS84)
Ask students: if res() returns 0.00833 degrees, how large is a pixel in meters at the equator? (~930m)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
What is a CRS?

A CRS defines how coordinates relate to real locations on Earth
Two broad families:

Geographic CRS — coordinates in degrees (longitude, latitude) on a spherical Earth model Example: WGS84 (EPSG:4326), used by GPS
Projected CRS — coordinates in meters (or feet) on a flat (2D) surface Example: EPSG:2169 (Luxembourg), UTM zones

Most downloaded satellite data uses WGS84; spatial analysis often requires a projected CRS



The Earth is curved, so projecting it onto a flat surface always introduces distortion
Geographic CRS is fine for storage and display; projected CRS is needed for distance/area calculations
A focal window of 3×3 in degrees is not 3×3 meters — this is why CRS matters for map algebra

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Checking the CRS

crs(r, describe = TRUE)   # human-readable summary

    name authority code  area             extent
1 WGS 84      EPSG 4326 World -180, 180, -90, 90




describe = TRUE gives a concise one-line summary: name, authority, code
The full WKT is what gets embedded in file metadata — this is what other software reads
If CRS is missing (NA), spatial operations may silently give wrong results

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Reprojecting with project()

Use project() to reproject a raster to a different CRS
The raster is resampled so that pixels align to the new grid


r_projected <- project(r, "EPSG:2169")

res(r)           # original: degrees

[1] 0.008333333 0.008333333

res(r_projected) # projected: meters

[1] 771.9715 771.9715




After projecting to EPSG:2169, res() returns meters (~927m here)
This is the same physical pixel size expressed in a different unit
project() involves interpolation, which slightly modifies values — only reproject when necessary
We will use this in Lesson 2 when we need focal windows in real-world units (meters)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Why CRS matters for analysis


Geographic (degrees)

Resolution of 0.00833°
A focal window of 3 cells ≈ 0.025°
Pixel “size” varies with latitude


Projected (meters)

Resolution of ~927m
A focal window of 3 cells = 2.8 km
Pixel size is constant everywhere




This difference becomes critical in Lesson 2 when we create focal windows
focalMat(r, d = 2000, "circle") requires the raster to be in meters to mean “2km radius”
Always check crs(r, describe = TRUE) and res(r) before doing spatial analysis

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
section: What does NA mean in a raster?
text:
What does NA mean in a raster?

In tabular data, NA means “value not recorded” for an observation
In raster data, NA has additional spatial meaning:

Outside the study area — pixels beyond the boundary of interest
Other, such as Sensor failure, Atmospheric effects etc.

NA pixels are not skipped in raster algebra — they propagate: 5 + NA = NA



This propagation behavior is different from what students may expect from tabular workflows
In raster operations, NA cells stay NA unless explicitly handled (na.rm = TRUE, mask, ifel)
Students will encounter this immediately when working with real satellite data (cloud cover)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
section: How NAs arise: study area boundaries
text:
How NAs arise: study area boundaries
r <- rast(system.file("ex/elev.tif", package = "terra"))
lux <- vect(system.file("ex/lux.shp", package = "terra"))

# show the bounding box vs the actual data extent
plot(r, main = "Values within Luxembourg boundary")
plot(lux, add = TRUE)






The raw raster extent (bounding box)







The raster grid is always rectangular — but the real data often covers an irregular shape
Cells outside the country boundary are NA
The bounding box (ext()) covers the whole rectangle

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
section: Working with NA: is.na() and mask()
text:
Working with NA: is.na() and mask()

# identify where NAs are
na_raster <- is.na(r)


# mask: set cells outside a vector boundary to NA
r_masked <- mask(r, lux)


# replace NA with a specific value (e.g. 0)
r_filled <- ifel(is.na(r), 0, r)



is.na() returns a Boolean raster: 1 where NA, 0 elsewhere
mask() takes a vector or raster boundary and sets everything outside to NA
ifel() is the raster equivalent of ifelse() for cell-by-cell conditional replacement
na.rm = TRUE in aggregation functions (mean, sum) ignores NAs, like in base R

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Edge effects in focal operations

Focal operations require a neighborhood around each cell
Cells at the raster edge do not have a full neighborhood
By default, this produces NA in the output border

r_foc     <- focal(r, w = 3, fun = mean)
r_foc_pad <- focal(r, w = 3, fun = mean, fillNA = TRUE)

plot(r_foc,     main = "fillNA = FALSE (default)")
plot(r_foc_pad, main = "fillNA = TRUE")






3×3 focal mean (note NA border)







3×3 focal mean with fillNA = TRUE







fillNA = TRUE pads the border with NAs before computing, so the output has the same extent as the input
For large windows the effect is more pronounced — a 11×11 window loses 5 cells on every side
This will matter in Lesson 2 when we compare focal window sizes

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Reading rasters from disk

# read a single-band GeoTIFF
r <- rast("data/elevation.tif")

# read a multi-band GeoTIFF
l7 <- rast("data/L7_ETMs.tif")

# read one specific band from a multi-band file
band3 <- rast("data/L7_ETMs.tif", lyrs = 3)


rast() reads all spatial metadata automatically (CRS, extent, resolution)
The data is not loaded into RAM by default — terra reads values on demand (lazy loading)
Use values(r) or as.matrix(r) to force loading all values into memory



Lazy loading is critical for large rasters that don’t fit in RAM
terra processes large rasters in chunks internally — students don’t need to manage this
Printing the object shows “source: …” confirming it’s backed by a file, not just in memory

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Writing rasters to disk

# write to GeoTIFF (all metadata is preserved automatically)
writeRaster(r, "data-out/elevation_out.tif")

# overwrite an existing file
writeRaster(r, "data-out/elevation_out.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

# specify the data type explicitly (default is Float32)
writeRaster(r, "data-out/elevation_byte.tif", datatype = "INT1U", overwrite = TRUE)


CRS, extent, resolution, band names and data type are all written into the file
Any software that reads GeoTIFF (QGIS, Python/rasterio, ArcGIS) will read the same metadata
Choosing the right datatype matters for file size — covered in Lesson 3



This is intentionally brief — the datatype/scale/offset topic is fully developed in Lesson 3
Reinforce: the file stores everything needed to reconstruct the raster — students don’t need separate sidecar files
Warn about overwrite = TRUE — it silently overwrites without a prompt

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

Explain the four sensor resolution types and their trade-offs
Distinguish and apply the four map algebra operation types in R
Understand why spectral indices are more robust than raw band values
Perform raster–vector operations: crop, mask, and extract
Connect focal operations to convolutions in image processing

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
The Four Resolutions

Spatial: Ground size of one pixel
Temporal: Revisit frequency
Spectral: Number & width of bands
Radiometric: Intensity levels (bit depth)

Trade-off example: Sentinel-2: 10 m · 5 days · 13 bands vs. MODIS: 500 m · daily · 36 bands — higher resolution in one dimension typically comes at the cost of another.


Flood mapping needs daily updates → MODIS; field-level crop mapping needs 10 m pixels → Sentinel-2
Hyperspectral sensors (EnMAP, AVIRIS) trade spatial resolution for hundreds of spectral bands
Radiometric resolution: 16-bit captures far more detail than 8-bit

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
From Sensor to Analysis
DN vs. Reflectance

Sensors record Digital Numbers (DN): raw detector output
DN values depend on illumination angle, atmospheric conditions, and sensor calibration — not directly comparable across dates or sensors

Calibration pipeline:



Step
Corrects for




DN → Radiance
Sensor gain & offset


Radiance → TOA Reflectance
Solar illumination angle


TOA → Surface Reflectance
Atmospheric scattering & absorption



Spectral indices are designed to work with reflectance: more sensor- and date-independent than raw DN.


Sentinel-2 Level-2A = surface reflectance (scaled ×10 000); Level-1C = TOA only — always check the product level
Computing NDVI on raw Level-2A integers still gives the right ratio (the scale cancels), but matters when comparing across sensors
How each step works:

DN → Radiance: per-band gain/offset scaling
Radiance → TOA Reflectance: normalise by solar irradiance & zenith angle
TOA → Surface Reflectance: radiative transfer model (e.g. Sen2Cor)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Introduction

Map algebra: operations that modify or summarize raster cell values
Four subclasses, differing in spatial scope:

Local — per-cell operations
Focal — central cell + neighborhood (typically 3×3)
Zonal — irregular regions defined by a second raster
Global — entire raster(s)




The four types differ in spatial scope — how many cells contribute to each output value
Which type gives mean elevation per municipality? Which smooths noise in an image?

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Operation Types — Illustrated


Figure 1: Local (one cell), Focal (3×3 neighborhood), Zonal (coloured regions), Global (entire raster)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Global Operation (1)

The most common global operations are descriptive statistics for the entire raster dataset such as the minimum, maximum or mean value.
For example: What is the mean elevation value for Luxembourg?



Common mistake: mean(r) computes a per-cell mean across bands (a local operation) — use global() for raster-wide statistics




Figure 2: Elevation of Luxembourg

# note: mean(r) does not work, since "mean" is used as a local operator
mean_elev <- global(r, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

mean_elev

              mean
elevation 348.3366

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Global Operation (2)

Another type of “global” operation is distance
This function calculates the distance from each cell to a specific target cell
For example, what is the distance from each cell to Luxembourg City, the capital of Luxembourg?



Why global, not local? A local operation uses only the value at (i,j) to produce the output at (i,j). Distance requires knowledge of the entire raster’s spatial extent and cell coordinates — no cell can be computed in isolation.

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Zonal

Zonal operations apply an aggregation function to multiple raster cells
A second raster with categorical values define the “zones”

What is the mean altitude per municipality?


Conceptually: spatial group_by + summarize
The zones raster must be integer/categorical — use rasterize() to convert vector polygons first



mean_vals <- zonal(r, zones, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Zonal — Result


Figure 3


The global operation can be seen as a special case of a zonal operation, where the only “Zone” is the entire dataset

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Local (1)

Local operations comprise all cell-by-cell operations in one or several layers.
For example, we can classify the elevation into values above and below a certain threshold



All arithmetic (+, -, *, /) and logical (>, <, &, |) operators work element-wise on rasters in terra
Boolean rasters are the foundation of masking and multi-condition selection (e.g. the solar panel task)



# first, create a boolean copy of the raster
r_bool <- as.logical(r)

mean_elev <- as.numeric(mean_elev)
mean_elev

[1] 348.3366

r_bool[r > mean_elev] <- FALSE
r_bool[r <= mean_elev] <- TRUE

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text: Local (1)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Local (2)

This type of (re-) classification is a very common operation
For more than 2 categories, we can use classify


cuts <- global(r, quantile, probs = c(0, .33, .66, 1), na.rm = TRUE)

r_classify <- classify(r, as.numeric(cuts))

# this next line just replaces the default labels with some custom ones
levels(r_classify) <- data.frame(ID = 0:2, category = c("low","mid","high"))

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text: Local (2)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Local (3)

Local operations are often used with multiple bands
For example, we could calculate the mean intensity values of red, green and blue:


l7 <- rast(system.file("tif/L7_ETMs.tif",package = "stars"))

names(l7) <- c("B", "G", "R", "NIR", "SWIR", "MIR")

l7_rgb <- l7[[c("R","G", "B")]]

plot(l7_rgb, nr = 1)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Local (3)

l7_rgb_mean <- mean(l7_rgb)

plot(l7_rgb_mean)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Local (4)

Local operations also work across bands — each output cell combines values from multiple input layers
For example, weighted brightness emphasises red over green and blue:

\[B = 0.5 \times R + 0.3 \times G + 0.2 \times B\]

brightness <- 0.5 * l7[["R"]] + 0.3 * l7[["G"]] + 0.2 * l7[["B"]]

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text: Local (4)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Spectral Indices: Why They Work
Healthy vegetation has a characteristic spectral signature:

Absorbs red (~650 nm): chlorophyll uses it for photosynthesis
Strongly reflects NIR (~800 nm): leaf cell structure scatters infrared light



Why not just use NIR alone? NIR is not unique to vegetation — bare soil, sand, and snow also have moderate-to-high NIR reflectance. What is unique to healthy vegetation is high NIR combined with low Red. NDVI exploits this contrast: a sandy surface has high NIR and high Red → NDVI ≈ 0; healthy vegetation has high NIR but low Red → NDVI close to 1. The normalization by (NIR + Red) also reduces the influence of varying illumination and atmospheric haze.



Numbers indicate Landsat TM bands: 1 Blue, 2 Green, 3 Red, 4 NIR, 5 SWIR1, 7 SWIR2 (band 6 thermal, off-chart). Source: seos-project.eu

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Normalized Difference Indices
\[\text{Index} = \frac{A - B}{A + B} \in [-1,\, +1]\]
Normalization reduces the effect of illumination differences.



Index
Formula
Detects




NDVI
(NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red)
Vegetation density


NDWI
(Green − NIR) / (Green + NIR)
Open water


NDSI
(Green − SWIR) / (Green + SWIR)
Snow & ice


NBR
(NIR − SWIR) / (NIR + SWIR)
Burn severity





All are local raster operations — same cell-by-cell arithmetic, different band combinations
Normalization cancels much of the multiplicative effect of illumination
NDWI has two conflicting definitions: Gao (1996) uses NIR/SWIR; McFeeters (1996) uses Green/NIR — always check which is cited
NBR is widely used for post-fire damage assessment with Sentinel-2 or Landsat

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Focal

While local functions operate on one cell focal operations take into account a central (focal) cell and its neighbors.
The neighborhood (also named kernel, filter or moving window) under consideration is typically of size 3-by-3 cells (that is the central cell and its eight surrounding neighbors), but can take on any other size or shape as defined by the user.
A focal operation applies an aggregation function to all cells within the specified neighborhood, uses the corresponding output as the new value for the central cell, and moves on to the next central cell



Key trade-off: larger window → more smoothing but larger NA border (edge effect)
fillNA = TRUE mitigates this by using whatever neighbors are available at the edges








Figure 4: Note how, depending on the size of your moving window, NA’s are produced. Source: Lovelace et al. (2019)




focal3by3 <- matrix(rep(1,9), ncol = 3)


focal11by11 <- matrix(rep(1,121), ncol = 11)


r_foc3 <- focal(r, focal3by3, fun = mean, fillNA = TRUE)

r_foc11 <- focal(r, focal11by11, fun = mean, fillNA = TRUE)









Figure 5











Note



Note how the output raster is smaller as the focal window is larger (edge effect)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Focal weights (1)

The focal weights we used above were square and evenly weighted


focal3by3

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    1    1
[2,]    1    1    1
[3,]    1    1    1



focal11by11  # same structure, 11×11

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Focal weights (2)

However, we can also create uneven weights:

For example, a laplacian filter is commonly used for edge detection.

laplacian <- matrix(c(0,1,0,1,-4,1,0,1,0), nrow=3) 

laplacian

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    0    1    0
[2,]    1   -4    1
[3,]    0    1    0


So are the sobel filters — shown on the next slide.

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Focal Operations = Convolutions
A focal operation with a weight matrix is a discrete convolution:
\[(\text{output})_{i,j} = \sum_{m}\sum_{n} w_{m,n} \cdot r_{i+m,\, j+n}\]
This is exactly the operation in convolutional neural networks (CNNs):



Hand-crafted kernel
Equivalent CNN concept




Gaussian blur
Smoothing / anti-aliasing layer


Sobel x/y
Edge detection layer


Mean filter
Average pooling



The key difference: in deep learning, kernels are learned from data rather than designed manually.


A CNN is essentially many stacked focal operations with learned kernels
The Sobel filter is exactly what a CNN’s first conv layer approximates when trained on natural images
Larger kernels → more smoothing = more bias, less variance

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
section: From cells to real world units (1)
text:
From cells to real world units (1)

We have been specifying our focal weights in terms of cell units
In most cases, it is more reasonable to work with real world units
The resolution of our raster is 0.008333333 (see res(r)) and since our raster is in WGS84, the units is “degrees”.
To work with more managable units, we can convert the raster to a projected CRS that uses “meters”, e.g. EPSG 2169



[1] 0.008333333 0.008333333



# Reproject to a "projected" CRS
r_2169 <- project(r, "EPSG:2169")

From cells to real world units (2)

The resolution of our new raster is 771.9714782 meters.
We can resample this to 1 km to simplify things


res(r_2169)

[1] 771.9715 771.9715

# first, create template raster with the same extent and 1km resolution
template <- rast(res = 1000, ext = ext(r_2169))

# then, resample to this template
r_2169 <- resample(r_2169, template)

Shapes: circle (d = radius), rectangle (d = dimensions), Gauss (d = sigma)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Focal functions in terrain processing

Focal functions are used to calculate the slope of a specific location, e.g. using the algorithm by Horn (1981)
Similarly, calculating the aspect (azimuth) of a location is a very typical task when dealing with elevation data
These algorithms are used so often, that they are implemented in a dedicated function (terrain())



terrain() is a convenience wrapper around a focal operation with a specific kernel
Horn’s algorithm uses a 3×3 weighted neighborhood to estimate the x/y gradient, from which slope and aspect are derived

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing

Focal functions in terrain processing

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Raster–Vector Operations
Vector data represents discrete geometries: points, lines, polygons — each with a geometry and attributes.
Three fundamental operations linking rasters and vectors:








Operation
Function
What it does




Crop
crop()
Reduce raster extent to bounding box of vector


Mask
mask()
Set cells outside vector geometry to NA


Extract
extract()
Get raster cell values at vector locations





crop() + mask() almost always used together: crop first (fast — clips extent), then mask (precise — removes cells outside geometry)
extract() bridges to tabular analysis — returns a data frame, not a raster

one_muni <- lux[5, ]           # one municipality polygon

r_crop <- crop(r, one_muni)
r_mask <- mask(r_crop, one_muni)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing

Why this matters

Storage space!
Sentinel-2 bands are stored as raw integers (UInt16, values ~0–15000)
The conversion to surface reflectance requires a scale and offset — documented in a separate XML file
GDAL reads individual JP2 files, not the full product → the conversion is never applied automatically
To work with S2 data correctly, we need to understand what scale and offset are and how to apply them



ESA’s design assumes the full SAFE product is used with their toolchain (SNAP, Sen2Cor) — scale/offset lives at the product level (MTD_MSIL2A.xml), not the file level
GDAL reads files, not products — so there is no mechanism for it to auto-apply the conversion
This is the motivating problem for this entire section

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Choosing a data type

Naively: value range determines the datatype
Better: transform values to fit a smaller type
Example: NDVI ∈ [−1, 1] → rescale to [0, 255] → store as Byte

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Rescaling / Transforming values
Min-max normalization maps any range \([\min(x), \max(x)]\) to a target range \([a, b]\):
\[x' = a + \frac{(x-\min(x))\times(b - a)}{\max(x)-\min(x)}\]
For NDVI ∈ [−1, 1] rescaled to [0, 255]:

\(x\) — measured value, \(x'\) — stored value
\(a = 0\), \(b = 255\) — target range
\(\min(x) = -1\), \(\max(x) = 1\)

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Precision (and lack thereof)

Only 255 distinct values → limited precision
Precision = \(\frac{1}{\text{scale}} = \frac{1}{127.5} \approx 0.008\)
Every stored NDVI is rounded to the nearest \(0.008\)
Is this enough? → depends on the use case

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
R Implementation for vectors

scale_minmax() applies the formula to a numeric vector:


scale_minmax <- function(
    x,
    a = 0,          # the minimum value of the new range (default 0)
    b = 255         # the maximum value of the new range (default 255)
    ){
  min_x = min(x)
  max_x = max(x)
  a + (x - min_x) * (b - a) / (max_x - min_x)
}

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Restoring the original values

A colleague receiving your file needs to know how to get back the original values
Invert the transformation using scale and offset: \[x = \frac{x' - 127.5}{127.5}\]

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
R implementation for rasters

GDAL supports scale/offset natively (pass directly to writeRaster())
Values are stored in file metadata and recognized during import
Formulas to derive them from the value range:

\[\begin{align}
\text{scale} &= \frac{b - a}{\max(x)-\min(x)} \\
\\
\text{offset} &= \frac{a \times \max(x) - b \times \min(x)}{\max(x)-\min(x)}
\end{align}\]
Note:

\(a\) and \(b\) refer to the target range
min and max could either be the theoretical or practical extremes: What are pros / cons of using either?

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
R implementation for rasters

scoff_params() works for vectors, but needs two adjustments for rasters:

min()/max() return per-cell values → use minmax() for global min/max
writeRaster() divides by scale and subtracts offset → both must be inverted



scoff_params <- function(x, a = 0, b = 255) {
  stopifnot(nlyr(x) == 1)
  mm     <- minmax(x)[, 1]
  scale  <- (b - a) / (mm[2] - mm[1])
  offset <- (a * mm[2] - b * mm[1]) / (mm[2] - mm[1])
  c(scale = 1 / scale, offset = -offset)
}

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
R implementation for rasters
Let’s import a raster, calculate the scale and offset values and use these values to write to disk

elev <- rast(system.file("ex/elev.tif", package="terra"))

so <- scoff_params(elev)

writeRaster(
  elev,
  "data-out/datatypes/INT1U.tif",
  overwrite = TRUE,
  scale  = so["scale"],
  offset = so["offset"]
  )

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
R implementation for rasters

GDAL embeds scale and offset in the file metadata
On import, any GDAL-based software restores the original values automatically
The stored INT1U bytes are invisible — you always get back the original range

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Lossless Compression

Even after choosing a compact datatype, files can be compressed further
Lossless compression reduces file size without changing any pixel values — the original data is perfectly recoverable
GeoTIFF supports several lossless algorithms via GDAL; DEFLATE is the most widely used


writeRaster(r, "output.tif", gdal = "COMPRESS=DEFLATE")


Compression is transparent to readers: any GDAL-based software (R, QGIS, Python) decompresses automatically on load
Combine datatype + compression for maximum savings: INT1U + DEFLATE can be 8× smaller than uncompressed FLT8S



DEFLATE is identical to the algorithm used in ZIP files — students will have intuition for it
LZW is an older alternative; ZSTD is newer and faster but less universally supported
Lossy compression (JPEG) exists for imagery but is rarely appropriate for analysis — pixel values change, which breaks indices and classification
“Transparent to readers” is the key selling point — no extra steps needed when loading the file

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Out-of-range reflectance values

hist(s2b)



Reflectance is bounded by definition: 0 (no reflection) to 1 (perfect reflection)
Yet the histogram shows values both below 0 and above 1

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
section: Why are values out of range?
text:
Why are values out of range?

Below 0 — ESA intentionally introduced a −1000 DN offset (processing baseline 04.00)

Dark surfaces (deep water, shadows) can have slightly negative reflectance after atmospheric correction
The offset shifts all DNs up to keep them positive on disk; subtracting it back out exposes those negatives
These values are physically meaningful — clipping them to 0 alters real data

Above 1 — clouds and saturated pixels exceed the calibration reference; these are true artefacts
The proper fix for both is SCL masking: clouds (8, 9), shadows (3), and water (6) are flagged and excluded
After masking, residual out-of-range values are rare; clipping is then a safe fallback

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Why clouds are a problem

Clouds reflect strongly across all bands — a cloudy pixel does not represent the surface below
Using cloudy pixels in analysis (e.g. NDVI, classification) introduces severe errors
Sentinel-2 L2A includes a Scene Classification Layer (SCL) → per-pixel quality flag generated automatically during atmospheric correction



Unlike thin haze, which affects values subtly, clouds completely obscure the surface — affected pixels must be excluded, not corrected
The SCL is generated by Sen2Cor (ESA’s atmospheric correction processor) using spectral rules and auxiliary data
It is not perfect — thin cirrus and cloud shadows in complex terrain can be misclassified — but it is the standard starting point

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Importing the SCL band

The SCL band is stored as a separate JP2 file in the R20m resolution folder (not R10m)
It follows the same naming convention as the spectral bands




The SCL is only available at 20m and 60m resolution — it must be resampled to match the resolution of the band stack you are masking
resample(scl, s2b, method = "near") aligns it to the target grid — nearest-neighbour is correct here because SCL is categorical

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Applying the cloud mask

# define which SCL classes are valid (cloud-free surface)
valid_classes <- c(4, 5, 6, 11)

# create a binary mask: TRUE where pixel is valid
cloud_mask <- scl %in% valid_classes

# apply to the reflectance stack
s2_masked <- mask(s2b, cloud_mask, maskvalues = FALSE)

# clip residual out-of-range values after masking
force_minmax <- \(x, min = 0, max = 1){ x[x < min] <- min; x[x > max] <- max; x }
s2_masked <- app(s2_masked, force_minmax)


%in% tests membership cell-by-cell and returns a Boolean raster
mask(..., maskvalues = FALSE) sets cells to NA wherever the mask is FALSE (i.e. cloudy)



Remind students that mask() was introduced in Lesson 1 — this is the same function, now applied for a real purpose
The result is a SpatRaster with the same bands as before but NA for all cloudy/shadowed pixels
Depending on cloud cover, this may remove a large portion of the image — this is expected, not an error

section: How much of the image is usable?
text:
How much of the image is usable?

# count valid (non-NA) pixels in band 1 as a fraction of total pixels
n_total <- ncell(s2_masked)
n_valid <- global(!is.na(s2_masked[[1]]), sum)[[1]]

cat(sprintf("Valid pixels: %.1f%%\n", 100 * n_valid / n_total))

Valid pixels: 74.6%



If usable coverage is low, consider:

Choosing a different date with less cloud cover
Mosaicking multiple acquisitions from nearby dates
Seasonal compositing: combine all cloud-free pixels from a season into one image




A common rule of thumb: discard scenes with > 20% cloud cover over your study area
But study area cloud cover matters more than full scene cloud cover — a scene can be 80% cloudy globally but cloud-free over your area of interest
Seasonal composites (e.g. median of all July scenes) are very robust and widely used in land cover mapping

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
The Spatial Context Problem

At pixel level, it is hard to distinguish forest from non-forest
Spatial context is essential: Humans use spatial context (texture, patterns, neighbors) to classify land cover



Figure 2

This is the core limitation of pixel-based classification.
Modern deep learning (CNNs) solves this automatically by processing image patches, but we’ll first show the manual approach to understand why spatial context matters.

title: Image Processing for Remote Sensing
text:
Approach 2: Adding Spatial Features

Focal operations as feature extractors: Focal operations aggregate neighborhood values, providing spatial context


i <- 5
focal_window <- matrix(rep(1, i^2), nrow = i)

# Calculate standard deviation in each neighborhood
ces1961_focal_sd <- focal(ces1961, focal_window, fun = "sd")


Pedagogical approach: Handcrafted focal features
Why we do this: - Explicit, understandable feature engineering - Shows what spatial context means (texture/variation) - Works with classical ML algorithms
Production approach: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) - CNNs learn optimal spatial filters automatically during training - First layer convolution weights = learned focal operations - Can learn multi-scale features (equivalent to multiple focal window sizes) - State-of-the-art: U-Net, DeepLabV3+, Vision Transformers
